name: Jaw surgery / orthognathic

card.summary: Corrective jaw surgery that repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw and chin for bite, airway and facial-balance goals; a legitimate surgical field that forums treat as the big structural lever.
card.aka: orthognathic surgery, corrective jaw surgery, double jaw surgery
card.note: Strong evidence is for bite, airway and function; cosmetic-only outcomes are less studied, and numbness, relapse and joint problems are documented.

quick.overview:
Orthognathic surgery is the medical term for jaw surgery that corrects the position of the upper jaw, lower jaw, chin or all three. It is used for underbites, overbites, open bites, asymmetry, jaw-joint problems and obstructive sleep apnoea, and it is also used to change facial proportions.

Looksmaxxing forums call it a hardmaxx procedure and discuss bimax, Le Fort I, genioplasty and related operations, with frequent questions about braces, insurance, recovery and complications. Medical literature documents functional outcomes and technique well, and is more limited on purely cosmetic goals.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons cut the jawbones from inside the mouth, move them to a planned position and fix them with titanium plates and screws, usually after orthodontic preparation. Virtual 3D planning, custom splints and patient-specific plates are increasingly used to transfer the plan to the operating room.
quick.risks: Reviews describe bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, jaw-joint effects, relapse, hardware problems and a recovery of weeks to months. A systematic review also estimated that body dysmorphic disorder is more common among orthognathic surgery patients than in the general community.

lead: Orthognathic surgery, also called corrective jaw surgery, reshapes the jaws and lower face to treat structural, growth, airway, jaw-joint and bite problems, and can also be used for facial balance and symmetry.[1] The operation is usually done through the mouth: bone is cut, moved and fixed in a new position, and it is typically coordinated with orthodontic treatment.[1][3]

Main procedures include the Le Fort I osteotomy for the upper jaw, the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy for the lower jaw, and genioplasty for the chin; surgeons may combine them in two-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery.[1][2] Reviews describe expanding indications for upper-airway obstruction, computer-assisted planning, patient-specific fixation and shifts in the orthodontic-surgical sequence over the past two decades.[4]

In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as one of the most consequential procedures, discussed alongside implants, rhinoplasty and orthodontics, with extensive talk about risk and surgeon choice.[15][16][17]

paras: The Le Fort I osteotomy moves the maxilla and is described in dedicated reviews that cover indications, contraindications, preoperative assessment, technique and complications.[5] The bilateral sagittal split osteotomy moves the lower jaw forward or back, and genioplasty repositions the chin and may be used alone or alongside jaw surgery.[1][3]

Genioplasty is described as an essential component when the chin position affects lower-face aesthetics, and contemporary reviews cover techniques, stability, fixation and complications.[3] Asymmetry cases are described as challenging, with 3D diagnosis and virtual planning increasingly helpful.[6]

A surgical team usually includes surgeons and orthodontists, with X-rays, photographs and 3D software used to predict the result and to help patients understand the plan.[1] Presurgical orthodontics has traditionally taken up to a year, with surgery-first approaches and clear aligners as newer alternatives.[1]

A systematic review of 12 studies found virtual planning accurate to under 2 mm on average in the maxilla and mandible in three planes,[7] and a prospective multicentre study of 65 patients evaluated a computer-aided surgical simulation protocol against actual outcomes.[9] A randomised trial compared periodontal health and quality of life with clear aligners versus fixed appliances after orthognathic surgery.[8]

Human research on orthognathic surgery covers planning accuracy, stability, complications, patient outcomes and sleep apnoea. A hierarchy-of-stability update reported that stability differs among surgical movements, with correction of asymmetry and chin repositioning very stable under rigid fixation.[10] A review of 655 patients examined the incidence of complications and problems after orthognathic surgery.[11] A 2016 individual-patient meta-analysis examined criteria associated with outcomes of maxillomandibular advancement for sleep apnoea.[12]

A systematic review found a weighted prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder of 11.2 percent in orthognathic surgery settings, compared with 1.9 percent in the adult community, and noted that the condition is poorly identified in practice.[13] Randomised trials have compared post-surgical orthodontic methods and maxilla-guided versus mandible-guided approaches with patient-specific implants.[8][14]

Wikipedia lists bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea and nerve-related numbness as the main risks, with the numbness usually temporary but occasionally permanent.[1] Initial healing is described as taking about two to six weeks, with complete bone healing taking longer.[1]

A forum member's long post summarising complications reported on forums and social media lists nerve damage, persistent numbness and altered sensation among the issues patients describe; another member who had a double-jaw operation for sleep apnoea reported good functional results but an unsatisfactory aesthetic outcome and later bone contouring.[17][16]

Forum threads describe jaw surgery as a major step for people with a recessed jaw, discussing whether to have a bimaxillary or single-jaw operation, when to start orthodontics and how age affects eligibility.[15] Members also discuss surgery abroad, recovery and complications, and compare jaw surgery with implants and other procedures.[16][17]

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known orthognathic cases.[1]
Hugo Obwegeser and Trauner are credited with the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia overview.[2]
Rigid titanium plate fixation reduces the need for long jaw immobilisation.[2]
Raffaini introduces lower-jaw surgery under local anaesthesia with sedation, shortening hospital stay.[1]
An updated hierarchy of stability for orthognathic procedures with rigid fixation is published.[10]
A prospective multicentre study evaluates computer-aided surgical simulation accuracy.[9]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org jaw surgery appears in threads on planning, braces, surgeon selection, recovery and complications, from first-time patients to people reporting revisions.[15][16][17]

claims.claim: Bimax or a single-jaw operation can fix a recessed jaw, and the result is often better than a jaw-jut test suggests.
claims.believers: A forum reply tells a prospective patient the result is usually better than what their jaw-jutting photos show because the photos cannot reflect the planned rotation, and suggests a combined operation.[15]
claims.experts: Reviews describe orthognathic surgery as correcting jaw discrepancies and note that planning software predicts the post-operative face; a systematic review reports average planning error under 2 mm.[1][7]

claims.claim: Jaw surgery carries serious risks that are underreported, including permanent numbness.
claims.believers: A forum author compiles complications from patient stories, listing nerve damage with long-lasting numbness as a prominent risk.[17]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that numbness is usually temporary and permanent numbness rare, and a 655-patient review examined complication incidence.[1][11]

claims.claim: Jaw surgery can improve function but disappoint cosmetically.
claims.believers: A forum member who had bimax for sleep apnoea describes a great functional outcome but a poor aesthetic one, with bony irregularities later shaved down.[16]
claims.experts: Reviews describe aesthetic balance as one goal of orthognathic surgery and planning software as a way to predict the result; no study in the reviewed sources directly compares functional and aesthetic outcomes in the same patients.[1][7]

claims.claim: Getting insurance to cover jaw surgery depends on proving a functional problem.
claims.believers: One poster asks whether to keep jutting the jaw so that pain could justify insurance coverage.[15]
claims.experts: Clinical sources list functional indications such as bite, joint and airway problems; coverage criteria are set by insurers and are not covered by the clinical literature reviewed.[1]
